headline: AI Scientist agent beats Opus 4.8 on replication
summary: Inherent's purpose-trained Faraday 27B agent reportedly outscores Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 at replicating published research.
display_body: Replication — taking a published paper and reproducing its results from scratch — is harder than it sounds, because papers routinely leave methodological details unstated, so a faithful redo demands the same open-ended, hypothesis-driven work as original research. The authors build Replica, a large task space of replication challenges, and an auto-generated rubric-based judge (a checklist grader) that they show is low-noise and agrees with human assessments of replication quality. Using that as a reward signal, they post-train Faraday, a 27B agent that calls coding agents as tools.
why: on held-out replication tasks Faraday reportedly surpasses Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 — a small, purpose-trained model beating two frontier systems at a concrete scientific-labor task, not a toy benchmark. Treat the head-to-head numbers as the authors' own until reproduced, but the result is a real data point in the "how close are autonomous researchers" debate.

headline: Research agents act like optimizers not scientists
summary: A systematic evaluation of seven frontier models on long-horizon R&D finds they behave like engineering optimizers, not autonomous researchers.
display_body: Most agent evaluations report only a final score, which hides where an agent gained or lost ground and whether it actually learned from earlier attempts. This study runs seven frontier models across 36 long-horizon R&D tasks under a framework that scores the process — how an agent frames a solution, executes it, and responds to feedback — and separately tests whether experience from one run improves later ones.
why: the verdict is a useful cold shower: current agents "operate more like engineering optimizers than fully autonomous researchers" — good at grinding a well-posed objective, weak at the reuse-of-experience that defines a scientist. Read against the Faraday result above, the two papers frame the live disagreement about how far this capability really extends.
affiliations: University of Chinese Academy of Sciences

headline: Benchmark tests agents on formally verified repos
summary: Vero is the first repository-level benchmark for agents that must jointly write code and a machine-checked proof it meets a spec.
display_body: AI coding agents give no guarantee their output is correct. Verified code generation raises the bar: the agent must emit both an implementation and a machine-checked proof that the code meets a formal specification (a proof assistant mechanically confirms it, leaving no room for a plausible-but-wrong answer). Prior benchmarks tested single functions, or proofs against code someone else wrote. Vero is the first to test both together at the whole-repository level — 43 multi-module instances drawn from real projects across Python, Dafny, Verus, and Coq.
why: "the agent wrote it and the tests pass" is a weak guarantee; "the agent wrote it and a proof checker verified it against a spec" is a strong one. A repository-scale benchmark is what tells us whether that stronger guarantee is within reach for real codebases rather than isolated snippets.

headline: Eval-awareness probe measures the prompt, not the model
summary: A widely cited probe for whether a model senses it is being tested tracks the prompt choice rather than the model or its scale.
display_body: A model that acts differently when it senses an evaluation would quietly corrupt the evals we trust, so researchers have tried to read that "sense" straight from activations: contrast the model's internal state on prompts that announce a test against prompts that don't, extract the difference as a direction, and report how cleanly it separates held-out cases — then compare that score across models and correlate it with scale. The catch, the author shows, is that "a prompt that announces an evaluation" is not one prompt but a choice among many, and the method never pins down which.
why: holding the task fixed and varying only that unstated choice, both the headline score and even the direction in which it trends with model size follow the prompt rather than the model. It's a clean warning that a widely cited interpretability result may be an artifact of prompt selection — exactly the kind of honest self-check the safety-eval literature needs.

headline: SAE ablation scores depend on where you measure
summary: Ablation-based sparse-autoencoder evaluation lets the dictionary under test choose its own measurement token, biasing comparisons.
display_body: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) try to name the concepts a model computes; the usual test of whether a discovered feature matters is to switch it off and see what changes. But a feature fires at many tokens, and the effect must be read at one of them — and the convention (measure where the feature fires hardest) means the dictionary being evaluated picks the measurement point. Take two SAEs Google released for the same model, match their features by similarity, and even near-identical features get measured at different tokens.
why: two dictionaries "compared" under the standard protocol are often not being measured on the same footing at all, so leaderboard-style SAE comparisons can reward measurement choices rather than better features. It's a distinct paper from the earlier "which SAE you trained decides causality" line, but it points the same way: interpretability's evaluation plumbing needs auditing before its scores can be trusted.

headline: Content-routed anchors give recurrent memory long recall
summary: MARCH adds content-routed state anchors so a fixed-size recurrent memory keeps long-range recall without a growing KV cache.
display_body: Transformers recall far-back tokens well because they keep a per-token memory (the KV cache) that grows with the input — but that means quadratic training cost and a cache that swells linearly at inference. Recurrent models fix the cost by squeezing all history into a fixed-size state, but they forget: new updates overwrite old associations, so only recent context survives. MARCH (Memory-Anchor Routing across Context History) adds content-routed state anchors — a fixed set of memory slots that incoming information is routed to by what it's about, so older associations are preserved in the slot they belong to rather than being overwritten.
why: the long-context/recurrent trade-off — cheap decoding versus reliable recall — is one of the central architectural tensions in scaling, and a fixed-size state that stops forgetting is a genuine attempt to get both. From a top Chinese lab consortium, it's worth watching whether the recall gains hold on the hardest retrieval tasks.

headline: Tree-structured speculative diffusion decoding
summary: DARTree extends an autoregressive correction head from chains to trees for training-free speculative diffusion decoding.
display_body: Speculative decoding speeds up text generation losslessly: a fast "drafter" guesses several tokens ahead and the real model verifies them in parallel. Diffusion drafters can propose a whole block at once, but their guesses aren't conditioned on which earlier draft tokens were actually chosen, so accuracy suffers. DARTree is a training-free method that extends a pretrained autoregressive correction head from a single draft chain to a tree: it builds a fixed-width candidate tree, scores all nodes at each depth in one batch, then applies correction along the best-fitting branch.
why: speculative decoding is one of the most practical inference speedups in deployment, and combining diffusion's parallel proposals with tree-structured verification is a concrete way to widen the guess without losing the causal correction that keeps it accurate.

headline: Training-free matrix-product reduction for inference
summary: RMM cuts an LLM's matrix multiplications at inference by keeping only informative contraction slices, no retraining.
display_body: Most of a transformer's inference cost is repeated large matrix multiplications. Reduced Matrix Multiplication (RMM) is a training-free, input-adaptive trick: for each product it keeps only the most informative slices along the shared "contraction" dimension (the axis summed over when multiplying two matrices), discarding the rest, controlled by a single retention-ratio knob that trades accuracy for speed smoothly and predictably. Weights are untouched.
why: across models from 1B to 70B, how much you can cut depends on family, task, and component — but tolerance often grows with scale, and under moderate reduction accuracy holds across generation and long-context settings. A drop-in lever with a predictable dial is exactly what practitioners can actually use.

headline: A minimal model unifies sudden learning and scaling laws
summary: A symmetry-derived quadratic form reproduces both plateau-then-drop learning and smooth power-law scaling.
display_body: Two puzzling training behaviors coexist: the loss can sit on a long plateau and then drop abruptly (learning in steps), while at the same time training curves follow smooth power laws (scaling laws) — and both appear in wildly different architectures, hinting that a few "collective variables" govern the dynamics regardless of the microscopic details. The authors show a symmetry fixes those variables: a layer is a sum over interchangeable units, so relabeling units changes nothing; that permutation symmetry, plus smoothness, forces a universal leading form near the small initial weights — a quadratic Tr[WWᵀA(x)] in which every architectural detail is packed into one "structure matrix" A(x).
why: if a single minimal model reproduces both sudden learning and smooth scaling from symmetry alone, it's a rare piece of theory that unifies two empirical mysteries deep learning has mostly just catalogued — the kind of result that can eventually make scaling behavior predictable rather than measured after the fact.

headline: Gemini 3.7 Flash undercuts predecessor by 50%
summary: Google ships Gemini 3.7 Flash with coding gains and halves the price of its three-week-old predecessor.
display_body: Google ships Gemini 3.7 Flash and halves the price of a model three weeks old. Google released Gemini 3.7 Flash with improved coding performance, undercutting its own predecessor's price by 50% barely three weeks after that predecessor launched — a cadence and price trajectory that says as much about the competitive squeeze on inference margins as about the model.

headline: Grok 4.6 matches OpenAI's best on price
summary: SpaceXAI's Grok 4.6 reportedly reaches parity with OpenAI's top model while charging less.
display_body: SpaceXAI's Grok 4.6 matches OpenAI's top model on quality and undercuts it on price. Grok 4.6 reportedly reaches parity with OpenAI's best model while charging less — the same pattern (frontier quality is being commoditized; price is now the battleground) playing out across every lab this week. Vendor-reported; independent benchmarks will tell whether "matches" holds.

headline: DeepSeek V4 Pro ships with open agent software
summary: DeepSeek releases the MIT-licensed V4-Pro-0813, open-sources its agent software, and raises API prices.
display_body: DeepSeek ships V4-Pro-0813, open-sources its agent software, and raises API prices. The MIT-licensed model card describes an official V4-Pro release with "greatly enhanced agentic capabilities," built on the V4-Pro Preview structure with a DSpark speculative-decoding module bolted on, and calls itself broadly competitive with the strongest proprietary models. Notably, DeepSeek simultaneously open-sourced its agent software and raised API prices — a "give away the weights, charge for the service" posture worth watching.

headline: Zhipu GLM-5.3 claims strongest open coding model
summary: Zhipu AI releases GLM-5.3, a coding model trained to find software vulnerabilities; weights are scheduled to open in about two weeks.
display_body: Zhipu's GLM-5.3 claims the strongest open coding model — and was trained to hunt vulnerabilities — but the weights aren't out yet. GLM-5.3 shares GLM-5.2's base, with all gains from extended post-training, and Zhipu says it leads open models on agentic coding. Distinctively, it was trained on data and environments for finding software vulnerabilities; working with Chinese security teams, Zhipu says it surfaced 2,436 flaws across 269 projects (some in code up to 40 years old), logged in a public registry. Important caveat: despite the "open-weights" framing, the weights are only scheduled to open in about two weeks, after security review — today it is API-only.

headline: Ling 3.0 Flash tops open models under 124B
summary: inclusionAI's Ling 3.0 Flash is the smartest open model under 124B parameters on Artificial Analysis's index.
display_body: On Artificial Analysis's Intelligence Index, Ling 3.0 Flash scores 38 — a large jump over its predecessor, level with Qwen3.6 27B while using far fewer active parameters, though still behind DeepSeek V4 Flash (52). Per Artificial Analysis, no smaller open model matches it; its hallucination rate on the Omniscience test fell from 97% to 44%, meaning it now declines to answer far more often when it lacks reliable grounding.

headline: Fully-open 1B model matches far larger ones
summary: DFM Mimir v1, a 1B model trained only on permissibly-licensed data, reportedly competes with models several times its size.
display_body: DFM Mimir v1, from the Danish Foundation Models group, is a 1B model on the Hierarchical Reasoning Model architecture, trained from scratch on 161 permissibly-licensed datasets. Across 20 English, math/code, and Danish benchmarks it reportedly competes with Qwen 3.5 4B and Gemma 4 E2B and sets a new Danish state of the art — a reminder that ethically sourced data only need not mean uncompetitive.

headline: Anthropic could be worth $2 trillion at IPO
summary: Reporting puts a potential Anthropic IPO valuation near $2 trillion.
display_body: Anthropic could be worth ~$2 trillion when it goes public. Reporting puts a potential Anthropic IPO valuation near $2 trillion — a number that, if it holds, would rank the lab among the most valuable companies on earth and underlines how far AI-lab valuations have detached from conventional revenue multiples.

headline: Gemini hits 1 billion users
summary: Google says Gemini has reached a billion users, its fastest-growing product ever.
display_body: Gemini hits 1 billion users, Google's fastest-growing product ever. Google says Gemini has reached a billion users faster than any prior product — distribution muscle (Search, Android, Workspace) turning into AI reach at a scale standalone competitors can't easily match.

headline: Fable 5 uptake hints at an enterprise price ceiling
summary: Slow corporate adoption of Fable 5 suggests willingness-to-pay for frontier AI may have a ceiling.
display_body: Sluggish Fable 5 uptake hints enterprise willingness-to-pay for frontier AI has a ceiling. Analysis of slow corporate adoption of the newest frontier tier argues that businesses may be reaching the limit of what they'll pay for marginal capability gains — the demand-side counterpart to this week's price-cutting on the supply side.
